lines.text: Before history had a name, people learned to farm, to build cities and to write. This is the ancient world, from the first temples to the fall of Rome.
On a hilltop in Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised rings of carved stone pillars, thousands of years before anyone farmed. Later, they buried the whole site.
In the Jordan valley, people settled at Jericho some eleven thousand years ago, and built a stone tower and walls, among the first signs of town life.
This was the New Stone Age, when people in many lands began to farm, keep animals and live together in villages.
At Catalhoyuk, in Turkey, mud-brick houses were packed so tightly that people came and went through their roofs, and painted their walls.
Farmers in dry lands learned to lead river water to their fields through canals. Without irrigation, the first great cities could never have been fed.
In southern Mesopotamia rose Sumer, a land of rival city-states. Its people built temple towers, dug canals and, in time, invented writing.
The plough let a farmer turn far more soil, first pulled by people and then by oxen, and the extra food fed growing towns.
Along the Nile, another civilisation was taking shape. Ancient Egypt would last some three thousand years, ruled by pharaohs and devoted to the afterlife.
Uruk grew into one of the first large cities in the world. Writing probably began here, and it was the home of the legendary king Gilgamesh.
Nearby stood Ur, with its great ziggurat and royal tombs full of treasure, a city later linked by tradition to Abraham.
Around this time the wheel appeared, first for making pots and then for carts. Within centuries, wheeled vehicles rolled across Europe and Asia.
In Sumer, scribes pressed reeds into wet clay to make wedge-shaped marks. Cuneiform would carry many languages for more than three thousand years.
Smiths learned to mix copper with tin to make bronze, harder than either. It gave its name to an age and sent traders far in search of tin.
Further east, along the Indus, people built planned cities with drains and standard weights, and wrote a script that nobody can read today.
Writing created a new kind of person, the scribe, trained to keep records. For thousands of years, only a few could read and write.
Egypt had its own writing, the hieroglyphs, carved on temples and tombs. How to read them was forgotten for centuries, until 1822.
In Greece, a settlement grew on the rock of the Acropolis. Athens would one day be the home of democracy, drama and philosophy.
Egyptians pressed the stems of a marsh plant into sheets of papyrus, the writing paper of the Mediterranean for thousands of years.
Their faith, with gods like Ra, Osiris and Isis and a king seen as divine, shaped everything from mummies to the pyramids.
On the island of Crete, the Minoans built the palace of Knossos, painted bright frescoes and traded across the eastern Mediterranean.
Back in the Indus valley, short strings of symbols were stamped on seals. Scholars still argue over whether they record a language at all.
Watching the Nile flood and the star Sirius rise, Egyptians made one of the first solar calendars: twelve months of thirty days, and five extra.
Then began Egypt's Old Kingdom, ruled from Memphis. Its kings built the first great pyramids, until drought brought royal power down.
At Saqqara, the official Imhotep stacked stone platforms into a step pyramid for King Djoser, the earliest large stone building on Earth.
Then came the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, the tallest building in the world for thousands of years, and the last ancient wonder still standing.
Beside the pyramids, a lion with a human face was carved from the bedrock. The Great Sphinx is usually linked to the pharaoh Khafre.
A cedar ship over forty metres long was buried in a pit beside the Great Pyramid, found again in 1954 and rebuilt piece by piece.
In the Indus valley, Mohenjo-daro flourished, a city of straight streets, brick houses and drains, carefully planned.
In Mesopotamia, the rival cities were joined into one state, the Akkadian Empire, the first of its kind in the region.
Its founder was Sargon of Akkad, often called the first empire builder, who brought Sumer and Akkad under one ruler.
On the Euphrates, Babylon began its long rise, a city that would become famous for its walls, temples and learning.
On clay tablets, poets wrote the Epic of Gilgamesh, the king of Uruk who seeks to live forever, one of the oldest stories we have.
Egypt, divided for a time, was reunited by kings from Thebes. The Middle Kingdom was a high point of Egyptian writing.
On the upper Tigris, Assyria began to grow, a kingdom that would become the largest and most feared empire of its age.
At Thebes, building began at Karnak, a forest of giant columns that pharaohs would enlarge for some two thousand years.
In Babylon, King Hammurabi made his city the leading power of Mesopotamia.
He had his laws carved on a stone pillar for all to see, setting out crimes, wages and punishments. Justice was now written and public.
In mainland Greece, warrior kings built fortified palaces at Mycenae and Pylos. Their world would live on in tales of Troy.
In Anatolia, the Hittites built an empire ruled from Hattusa, and spoke the earliest Indo-European language we have in writing.
Far to the east, the Shang dynasty ruled along the Yellow River, casting fine bronzes and writing on oracle bones.
In the Aegean, the volcano of Thera, today's Santorini, exploded. It buried the town of Akrotiri and may have harmed the Minoans of Crete.
Egyptians placed the Book of the Dead in their tombs, spells and prayers to guide the soul through the underworld.
Now came the New Kingdom, the height of Egypt's power, when pharaohs ruled an empire from Nubia to Syria.
One of its greatest rulers was a woman. Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh, sent traders to the land of Punt and built a grand temple at Deir el-Bahari.
Instead of pyramids, the pharaohs were now buried in rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings, their walls painted for the afterlife.
Her stepson Thutmose the Third, ruling alone, led campaign after campaign into the Levant and took Egypt to its widest reach.
In Greece, palace scribes kept their accounts in Linear B. When it was deciphered in 1952, it turned out to be an early form of Greek.
Then a pharaoh broke with tradition. Akhenaten raised the sun disc Aten above all other gods, and moved his court to a new city.
That city was Amarna, built from nothing in the desert and abandoned soon after, leaving clay letters of royal mail behind.
From a sculptor's workshop there came the painted bust of his queen, Nefertiti, still one of the most famous faces of the ancient world.
After Akhenaten came a boy king, Tutankhamun, who died in his teens. His nearly untouched tomb would make him the most famous pharaoh of all.
Ramesses the Second ruled Egypt for more than sixty years, a warrior and a tireless builder of temples.
In Syria, his army clashed with the Hittites at Kadesh, one of the earliest battles whose tactics we know well.
In the south, four giant seated statues of Ramesses were cut into a cliff at Abu Simbel, temples moved to higher ground in the 1960s to save them.
After years of fighting, Egypt and the Hittites made peace. Their treaty is the oldest whose text survives, in both languages.
In Greek memory, this was the time of the Trojan War, the ten-year siege of Troy. Whether it happened as Homer tells it is still debated.
In China, the oldest known characters were scratched on oracle bones, the start of a writing system still used today.
Then the Bronze Age world fell apart. Cities from Greece to Syria were burned or abandoned, trade stopped, and in places writing vanished.
In Nubia, the Kingdom of Kush rose on the upper Nile. Its kings would one day rule Egypt itself, and build pyramids of their own.
The traders of Tyre and Byblos used just twenty-two letters. Their alphabet became the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic.
The Greeks borrowed it and added letters for vowels, making the first full alphabet, the parent of Latin and Cyrillic.
In the Peloponnese, Sparta grew into a city of soldiers, ruled by two kings and famous for its hard military training.
To the north lay Macedon, a Greek kingdom that, centuries later, would conquer Persia under Alexander.
On the slopes of Mount Parnassus, at Delphi, a priestess spoke for Apollo, and cities and kings came to ask her advice.
The Greeks honoured Zeus, Athena, Apollo and the other Olympian gods, with festivals, sacrifices and myths told by poets.
At Olympia, games were held in honour of Zeus every four years, and the warring cities agreed to lay down their arms while they ran.
In Italy, tradition says, a small settlement was founded on the Tiber. Rome would grow to rule the whole Mediterranean.
From its early days, Rome had a council of elders, the Senate, which would guide the city for more than a thousand years.
In Greece, the poet known as Homer gave form to the old stories. Little is known about him, or even whether he was one person.
The Iliad tells of the anger of Achilles in the last year of the Trojan War. For centuries, Greek children learned from it.
The Odyssey follows Odysseus on his long voyage home, past monsters and storms, a story writers have borrowed ever since.
At Nineveh, the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal gathered a great library of clay tablets. When the city burned, the fire preserved them.
In Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar the Second captured Jerusalem and rebuilt his capital in splendour, with the blue Ishtar Gate.
On the island of Lesbos, the poet Sappho sang of love and longing. Only fragments survive, but the ancients ranked her among the best.
In Miletus, Thales looked for natural causes rather than the will of the gods, and is often called the first Western philosopher.
Greek writers told of terraced gardens in Babylon, the Hanging Gardens. No Babylonian text mentions them, and they may never have existed.
In Rome, the Forum became the heart of the city, an open square of temples and courts where speeches, trials and triumphs took place.
In Persia, Cyrus the Great conquered the Medes, Lydia and Babylon, and let the peoples he ruled keep their own customs and gods.
Near Naples, the town of Pompeii was growing, unaware that one day a volcano would bury it and keep it for us.
Pythagoras of Samos founded a community of thinkers in southern Italy. A famous theorem about triangles still carries his name.
The empire Cyrus founded stretched from Egypt to the Indus, held together by governors, a royal road and tolerance.
Rome threw out its kings and became a republic, governed by elected magistrates and the Senate.
In Athens, the reforms of Cleisthenes let citizens meet in an assembly and vote on laws and war themselves. Democracy was born.
When Greek cities in Asia rebelled against Persia, half a century of war began between the empire and the Greeks.
In the theatre of Athens, Sophocles won prize after prize. His Oedipus the King and Antigone are still performed today.
Pericles led Athens through its golden age, championing democracy and the building of the Parthenon.
At Marathon, the Athenians drove a Persian landing force into the sea. The story of a runner carrying the news gave us the marathon.
Herodotus travelled the eastern Mediterranean and wrote the story of these wars, full of tales of distant peoples. He is called the father of history.
Ten years later Persia came again. At Thermopylae, the Spartan king Leonidas and a small force held a narrow pass against a huge army.
That same year, in the strait of Salamis, the Greek fleet crushed a larger Persian one, and Greece was safe.
In the streets of Athens, Socrates questioned everyone about justice and virtue. He wrote nothing, but his pupils made him immortal.
On the island of Kos, Hippocrates taught that illness has natural causes. Doctors still take an oath that bears his name.
The Athenian general Thucydides wrote the history of his own war, looking for causes in human ambition rather than in the gods.
In Rome, the first laws were written on the Twelve Tables and set up in public, so that ordinary citizens could know them.
On the Acropolis, the Parthenon was completed, a marble temple to Athena that still stands as a symbol of Athens.
Then Athens and Sparta went to war. The Peloponnesian War lasted almost thirty years and left Athens beaten.
Early in the war, a plague swept the crowded city, killing a large share of its people, and Pericles himself.
Plato, the pupil of Socrates, founded the Academy and wrote dialogues such as the Republic, asking how a city should be governed.
In 399 BCE, an Athenian jury found Socrates guilty of corrupting the young. He was put to death with a cup of hemlock.
Plato's student Aristotle wrote on logic, ethics, politics and living things, and shaped thought in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.
Aristotle's most famous pupil became king of Macedon at twenty. Alexander the Great conquered Persia and marched as far as India.
In Egypt, he founded Alexandria, a port that would become one of the largest and most learned cities of the ancient world.
At Gaugamela, on an open plain in today's Iraq, he defeated the Persian king Darius, and the empire of Cyrus fell.
In Alexandria, Euclid gathered the geometry of his day into the Elements, a textbook used for more than two thousand years.
Alexander died at thirty-two, and the Hellenistic age began, as Greek culture spread across the Middle East under his successors.
Meanwhile, Rome began the Appian Way, a paved military road heading south. Parts of it are still walked today.
In Egypt, Alexander's general Ptolemy founded a Greek dynasty that would rule from Alexandria until Cleopatra.
In Athens, Zeno taught a new philosophy, Stoicism: we cannot control events, only how we judge them and how we act.
In Syracuse, Archimedes worked out the laws of floating bodies and the lever, until he was killed when the Romans took his city.
The Ptolemies founded the Library of Alexandria, meant to hold every book in the world. Its scholars measured the Earth and edited Homer.
On Rhodes, a giant bronze statue of the sun god was raised. The Colossus stood for only about half a century before it fell.
At the harbour of Alexandria, a great lighthouse rose on the island of Pharos, guiding ships for well over a thousand years.
In the west, Rome and Carthage went to war over Sicily. Rome built its first great fleet, won, and gained its first province overseas.
Carthage's answer was Hannibal, the general who would cross the Alps with elephants to bring the war to Italy.
Rome's answer was Scipio, who would drive Carthage out of Spain and carry the war to Africa.
The Second Punic War began. For years Hannibal's army roamed Italy, while Rome struck back abroad.
At Cannae, Hannibal surrounded and destroyed a much larger Roman army, one of the worst defeats Rome ever suffered.
But at Zama, in North Africa, Scipio finally beat Hannibal. Carthage lost its empire, and Rome ruled the western Mediterranean.
Roman builders mixed lime and volcanic ash into a concrete that set hard even under water, and raised domes, harbours and aqueducts.
In Egypt, a royal decree was carved in three scripts on one stone. Two thousand years later, the Rosetta Stone unlocked the hieroglyphs.
In a third and last war, Rome besieged Carthage, destroyed the city and turned its lands into a Roman province.
On the island of Milos, a sculptor carved a marble goddess, the Venus de Milo, now admired in the Louvre without her arms.
In Rome, Cicero, the greatest orator of his age, rose to be consul, and defended the Republic in speeches and letters.
The gladiator Spartacus led enslaved people in revolt, defeating Roman army after army before he was crushed.
Somewhere in the Greek world, a bronze machine of many gears was made to model the heavens. Nothing like it is known for a thousand years after.
Then came Julius Caesar, the general whose ambition would bring the Republic to an end.
Virgil, a poet of the countryside, would one day write Rome's own epic.
In Egypt, Cleopatra, last of the Ptolemies, would ally with Caesar and then Mark Antony to keep her kingdom free.
And Caesar's great-nephew Octavian, later called Augustus, would become the first Roman emperor.
Caesar conquered Gaul, roughly today's France and Belgium, in eight years of war, and came back rich and dangerous.
When the Senate turned against him, he crossed the Rubicon and beat Pompey in a civil war fought across the Mediterranean.
After Caesar was murdered on the Ides of March, his heir Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra at sea, off Actium.
Now sole ruler, Augustus founded the Roman Empire, which would stretch from Britain to Egypt and spread roads, law and Latin.
Two centuries of peace followed, the Pax Romana, when trade and cities flourished across the empire.
For Augustus, Virgil wrote the Aeneid, the tale of the Trojan hero whose descendants would found Rome. He died before it was finished.
Claudius, thought an unlikely emperor, governed well, and under him Rome conquered southern Britain.
After a year of civil war, the general Vespasian took the throne, restored the finances and began the Colosseum.
Earlier, the young Caligula had come to power popular, but his short and cruel reign ended in his murder by his own guard.
Nero, who loved music and the stage, was emperor when Rome burned. A revolt of his generals drove him to suicide.
Trajan, born in Spain, conquered Dacia and campaigned in the east, and the empire reached its greatest size.
His successor Hadrian gave up some of those conquests and travelled the provinces, making the empire's borders firm.
In the year 79, Vesuvius erupted. Pompeii and Herculaneum vanished under ash, preserving everyday Roman life in remarkable detail.
A year later the Colosseum opened in Rome, a vast arena where crowds watched gladiators and animal hunts.
Marcus Aurelius spent his reign defending the northern frontier, and wrote private notes, the Meditations, still read today.
Across northern Britain, Hadrian's soldiers built a stone wall with forts and gates to mark the edge of the empire.
In Rome, the Pantheon was rebuilt with a great concrete dome open to the sky, the largest of its kind for centuries.
Marcus's son Commodus fought in the arena as a gladiator, and was killed in a plot, as the long peace came to an end.
After a long crisis, Diocletian split the empire among four rulers, reformed taxes, and persecuted the Christians.
Constantine reunited the empire, favoured Christianity and founded a new capital in the east, Constantinople.
In 313 he and his fellow emperor agreed in Milan to let Christians worship freely, ending the persecutions.
Theodosius made Christianity the religion of the state. He was the last to rule both halves of the empire.
After him the east went its own way. The Byzantine Empire would last another thousand years, ruled from Constantinople.
In the west, the Huns under Attila raided both empires, and invaded Gaul and Italy.
In 410, the Visigoths of Alaric plundered Rome for three days, the first time in about eight hundred years the city had fallen.
And in 476, the commander Odoacer removed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus. In the west, Rome's empire was over.
The cities fell, but their writing, laws and ideas lived on, and still shape the world today.
